summary: Describes the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS), used to digitally sign, digest, authenticate, or encrypt arbitrary message content. It replaces RFCs 2630 and 3211 and was later replaced by RFC 3852.

plainLanguage.summary: CMS is a standard way to put a message in a locked or signed envelope. It lets anyone check who sent it, or keep it secret.

questions: how to sign or encrypt messages with cms
what is the difference between cms signed-data and enveloped-data
what content types does cms define
subtitle: A general envelope format for signing, encrypting, digesting and authenticating any message content.

tldr.problem: Applications such as secure email need one common way to sign, digest, authenticate or encrypt arbitrary data, even nested several layers deep.
tldr.mechanism: The Cryptographic Message Syntax wraps content in a ContentInfo structure with a content type identifier, and defines six content types: data, signed-data, enveloped-data, digested-data, encrypted-data and authenticated-data.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3369 obsoleted RFC 2630 and RFC 3211, adding password-based key management and an extension point for new key management schemes, and was later replaced by RFC 3852.

today: RFC 3369 has been obsoleted by RFC 3852, which is the later CMS specification. It had itself replaced RFC 2630 and RFC 3211.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) is used to digitally sign, digest, authenticate or encrypt arbitrary message content. It is an encapsulation syntax: one envelope can be nested inside another, and one party can sign data that was already encapsulated. Arbitrary attributes, such as signing time, can be signed along with the content, and others such as countersignatures can be attached to a signature.

CMS values are described in ASN.1 and encoded with BER. The syntax is derived from PKCS #7 version 1.5 (RFC 2315) with backward compatibility kept wherever possible. This document obsoletes RFC 2630 and RFC 3211: it folds in password-based key management, adds an extension mechanism for new key management schemes, adds version 2 attribute certificate transfer, and deprecates version 1 attribute certificates.

Specific cryptographic algorithms are deliberately not covered here. They were moved to a separate document (RFC 3269), and CMS does not require any particular algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: CMS is the shape of the envelope, not the lock. Different locks can be chosen for different jobs.

sections.title: Overview and the ContentInfo Wrapper
sections.content:
Everything in CMS sits inside a protection content called ContentInfo, which is a pair: a contentType object identifier and the content itself. This document defines six content types: data, signed-data, enveloped-data, digested-data, encrypted-data and authenticated-data. Further types can be defined elsewhere, though the ASN.1 type they use SHOULD NOT be a CHOICE.

A conforming implementation MUST implement ContentInfo and the data, signed-data and enveloped-data types; the others MAY be implemented. The data type is just an arbitrary octet string, such as an ASCII text file, and its interpretation is left to the application. It is normally wrapped inside one of the other types.

The design aims for single-pass processing with indefinite-length BER encoding, which helps with large or piped content. The exception is that signed attributes and authenticated attributes must be DER-encoded so a recipient can verify content with unrecognized attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: Every CMS message is a labelled box. The label says what kind of box it is, and some boxes can hold other boxes.

sections.title: Signed-data
sections.content:
The signed-data type carries content plus zero or more signatures, and any number of signers can sign in parallel. For each signer, a message digest of the content is computed, then signed with the signer's private key, and the result goes into a SignerInfo. The SignedData value holds the version, the digest algorithms, the encapsulated content, optional certificates and CRLs, and the signer infos.

If signedAttrs are present, they MUST include a content-type attribute and a message-digest attribute, and they are what actually gets signed, using their DER encoding. They are required whenever the content type is not id-data. The signer is identified either by issuer name and serial number, or by the X.509 subject key identifier. The recipient MUST NOT rely on digest values computed by the originator and must recompute them.

If eContent is omitted, the result is an external signature, where the signed data travels separately. The RFC also warns about subtle incompatibilities with PKCS #7 when the encapsulated content is not of the data type.
sections.plainLanguage: Signing is like putting your personal stamp on a letter. Anyone can look at the stamp to see it was you and that nobody changed the words afterward.

sections.title: Enveloped-data and Key Management
sections.content:
The enveloped-data type holds encrypted content together with the content-encryption key encrypted for one or more recipients. A random content-encryption key encrypts the content once, and the key is then encrypted separately for each recipient, giving each of them a digital envelope. Each recipient can use a different key management technique, represented by a RecipientInfo choice.

  • ktri (key transport): the key is encrypted in the recipient's public key.
  • kari (key agreement): a pairwise key derived from the sender's private key and the recipient's public key encrypts the content-encryption key.
  • kekri: a previously distributed symmetric key-encryption key is used.
  • pwri: the key-encryption key is derived from a password or other shared secret.
  • ori: an extension point for other key management techniques defined in future documents.

Implementations MUST support key transport, key agreement and previously distributed symmetric keys, and MAY support password-based and other techniques. All implementations MUST gracefully handle unimplemented algorithms, versions and ori alternatives. The recipientInfos field comes before the encrypted content so processing can be single pass.
sections.plainLanguage: You lock the message with one secret key. Then you make a separate copy of that key for each friend, locked in a way only that friend can open.

sections.title: Digested, Encrypted and Authenticated Data
sections.content:
The digested-data type is content plus a message digest of it. It provides integrity and typically becomes the input to enveloped-data. A recipient compares the digest with one it computes independently.

The encrypted-data type is encrypted content with no recipients and no encrypted keys, so keys MUST be managed by other means. The RFC says its typical use is encrypting content for local storage, perhaps with a key derived from a password.

The authenticated-data type carries content, a message authentication code (MAC) and the MAC key encrypted for each recipient. The MAC is computed over the content, or, if authenticated attributes are present, over their DER encoding, which must include the content-type and message-digest attributes. Recipients MUST NOT rely on MAC or digest values computed by the originator.
sections.plainLanguage: A digest is like a fingerprint of the message. A MAC is a fingerprint that only people with the secret key can make, so you can tell nobody tampered with it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC lists what implementations must protect: the signer's private key, because compromise permits masquerade; and the key management private key, key-encryption key and content-encryption key, because compromise can disclose all content protected with them. For authenticated data, a compromised MAC key permits undetectable modification.

Key management for MAC keys must itself provide data origin authentication. The RFC says RSA and Ephemeral-Static Diffie-Hellman do not, while Static-Static Diffie-Hellman does when both public keys are bound to identities in X.509 certificates. When more than two parties share a MAC key, data origin authentication is lost, since any of them can compute a valid MAC.

Content-encryption keys, MAC keys, IVs and padding must be randomly generated, and weak pseudo-random generators can reduce security to a small searchable set. If the key-encryption algorithm is weaker than the content-encryption algorithm, the weaker one sets the effective security. Countersigners should verify the original signature before countersigning it.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep your keys safe, make them with truly random choices, and do not lock a strong box with a weak padlock.

items.label: id-data
items.desc: Arbitrary octet strings; meaning is left to the application.

items.label: id-signedData
items.desc: Content plus any number of signatures.

items.label: id-envelopedData
items.desc: Encrypted content plus encrypted keys for one or more recipients.

items.label: id-digestedData
items.desc: Content plus a message digest of it.

items.label: id-encryptedData
items.desc: Encrypted content with no recipients; keys managed by other means.

items.label: id-ct-authData
items.desc: Content, a MAC, and the MAC key encrypted for each recipient.

viz.caption: RECIPIENTINFO CHOICES AND THEIR VERSIONS (RFC 3369, SECTION 6.2)

items.label: KeyTransRecipientInfo
items.desc: Key transport. Version 0 with issuer and serial number, or 2 with a subject key identifier.

items.label: KEKRecipientInfo
items.desc: Previously distributed symmetric key. Version always 4.

items.label: PasswordRecipientInfo
items.desc: Password-based. Version always 0. Specified in RFC 3211.

items.label: OtherRecipientInfo
items.desc: Extension point for future key management techniques.
